Field Guide · Native UI in RustRune rev 6231f17 · November 2026

A course in eight lessons

Rune, from zero

Build real, GPU-drawn desktop apps in Rust: from a light switch on a spring to fire, liquid glass and shockwaves. Along the way you compile your first executable and wrap it into a Mac app you can double-click.

For readers who finished Rustlings and know Python or JS/TS. Every snippet on this page is cut from code that compiled against the pinned rev, and every moving picture is a recording of that code running on a Mac's Metal GPU.

Before you start

How to work this guide

Goal: by the end you've built six small Rune apps across eight lessons, bundled one as a double-clickable .app, and written a headless test suite that drives one of them without a window. Some apps carry more than one lesson: Lesson 5 tests the swipe app from Lesson 4.

Learning style: hybrid, with the scaffolding fading as you go. Lesson 1 is a worked example: you read and run a finished app, because you can't fill in the blanks of something you've never seen whole. Lessons 2-4 are guided: stubs with hint ladders. Lessons 5-8 are closer to solo: a name, a shape and an expectation.
Prerequisites: Rustlings (ownership, structs, enums, match, closures, iterators), a terminal, and an Apple-silicon Mac for the bundling and effects lessons.

Follow it in order. Run every command and check that you get the expected result before you move on. Try each TODO(you) before you open its Solution: the Solution is an answer key for checking a real attempt, not a walkthrough. If anything in STOP conditions happens, stop and ask. Don't improvise.

Drift check (run first) grep -n 'rev = ' Cargo.toml must print 6231f1753432550c72f0cd52dab3a08612ce4162 on both lines. Rune is pre-release, so if you move the rev, an API on this page can change name. Treat a mismatch as a STOP condition.

Why this matters

Most desktop apps you've used are web pages in a box. Electron ships a whole browser, and Tauri borrows the system's. Rune doesn't draw with a browser at all. It lays out boxes with Taffy (the flexbox algorithm, in Rust), shapes text with Parley, and paints every pixel itself through wgpu, which talks to Metal on a Mac. The result is one native executable with no DOM, no CSS and no JavaScript runtime.

That changes what you need to know. In JS the browser decides when to repaint and the bundler hides compilation. In Rune you describe the screen as a pure function of your state, the framework diffs it and springs anything that moved, and cargo turns all of it (Rune, its dependencies, your code) into one machine-code file. Lesson 1 opens that box.

There's one more reason. Every Rune app can run headless: it renders PNGs and video and drives scripted input with no window. That's how you'll test it (Lesson 5), and it's how every recording on this page was made.

Current state

tutorial/ is a self-contained Cargo package inside this repo. The solutions live in src/bin/ (one file per lesson, each its own program), the exercise stubs in examples/, and the one piece of shared code, the effects compositor, in src/gfx.rs.

The exemplar is Rune's own examples/hello at the pinned rev. Lesson 1 is that app with a calculation pulled out and the sections labelled. You can read it at anomalyco/rune examples/hello. Don't edit anything in the Rune repo. It's a dependency, not part of this course.

The dependency block is the part of Cargo.toml that matters (lines 7-13):

[dependencies]
rune = { git = "https://github.com/anomalyco/rune", rev = "6231f1753432550c72f0cd52dab3a08612ce4162" }

[target.'cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))'.dependencies]
wgpu = { version = "30", default-features = false, features = ["vulkan", "dx12"] }

Concepts you'll need

  • Compiling vs. interpreting. Rust turns source into a machine-code file before anything runs. Python and Node read your source at run time. You need this to know what cargo build produces and why the result runs on a Mac with no Rust installed. Taught in Lesson 1.
  • State → view → event → state. The whole Rune model (Elm style). Taught in Background and Lesson 1.
  • Closures that capture by move. Every event handler is one. Assumed from Rustlings (exercises/closures), and revisited in Lesson 2.
  • Flexbox. Rune's row/col follow CSS flexbox rules, so what you know from the web carries over. Taught in Lesson 2.

Scope

In scope (the only files you change): your own copies of the exercises under tutorial/examples/ (or new files in tutorial/src/bin/), and tutorial/scripts/*.json if you write your own replay scripts.

Out of scope (don't touch):

  • tutorial/src/gfx.rs: the effects compositor. You read it in Lesson 6. Writing GPU passes is its own course, and the stretch goal at the end points there.
  • The repo root (Cargo.toml, src/): the six-experiment app that inspired this course. It shares the repo but not the package.
  • Rune itself: a git dependency at a pinned rev. The Rune team doesn't take PRs. Bugs go to its issues.
  • The web target (WebGPU canvas): experimental. In Chrome and Helium it clipped the canvas and dropped effects, so this course is native only.

Background concepts

The whole model on one page

What is Rune? (First principles)

Picture a flipbook. Each page is drawn fresh from a description ("the switch is on, the knob is at the right"), and the animator never erases and redraws one line. Rune works the same way. You write one function that describes the whole screen from your data, and Rune calls it again whenever the data changes. In the jargon, this is a declarative, immediate-mode view with a retained diff. Rune keeps the previous page, compares, and animates what moved.

The pieces you'll use:

  • State (a struct you write). What: everything the app knows. When: created once by init and changed only by handlers.
  • view(&State, &mut Cx<State>) -> El. What: the screen as a tree of elements. When: Rune calls it after every change. Returns: the root El.
  • Builders: el(), row(), col(), text(..). What: make an El, then chain methods (.size(), .fill(), .child()…). Returns: El, by value, so every chain consumes and returns.
  • Handlers: .on_press(|s: &mut State| ..), .on_drag(..). What: the only place state changes. When: between frames, with exclusive access to the state.
  • AppSpec + rune::run. What: wires title, size, init, view and named scenes into a running app (window or headless).

Real-world analogy: a theatre lighting board. The cue sheet (state) says what should be lit, the board (view) turns that into fader positions, and the fade time (a spring) is how the lights get there. You never animate a fader by hand.

How one tap flows

1. view(&state)         → El tree      Calculation
2. layout + draw        → pixels       Orchestration
3. tap the switch       → on_press     Action
4. state.on flips       → new data
5. view(&state) again   → new El tree  Calculation
6. diff old/new by key  → knob x 2→18
7. spring, ~0.25 s      → it glides    Orchestration

Classification note. This course sorts every piece of code into one of three kinds, from Grokking Simplicity, plus two wiring roles:

DataThe footage in the vault. State, constants. Inert.
CalculationA colour-grade preset: same frame in, same frame out. view, knob_x.
ActionA live take: depends on when and how often. Handlers, poll.
OrchestrationThe edit: sequences takes, shoots nothing. Rune's frame loop.
MainThe director: one per film. fn main.

Prefer data to calculations, and calculations to actions. In Rune that rule is built in: the view is a calculation by type signature.

1

Worked example · Concepts: cargo, compiling, binaries, state → view

Compile your first app

A light switch, and the trip it takes from a .rs file to a program your Mac can run.

Concept: compiling

Picture it first. Python is a live translator who reads your script aloud to the CPU, line by line, every time you run it. Rust is a translator who takes the whole book away and comes back with a finished edition in the CPU's own language. It's slower to get the first copy, but nobody needs the translator in the room after that.

What is it? Compiling turns source code into machine code: CPU instructions packed into an executable file (on a Mac, a Mach-O file). cargo is Rust's all-in-one tool. If you know Node, it's npm, tsc and your bundler in one:

JS / TSRust
package.jsonCargo.toml
package-lock.jsonCargo.lock (exact versions of every crate)
.nvmrcrust-toolchain.toml (pins compiler 1.99.1)
node_modules/~/.cargo/registry + ~/.cargo/git (sources)
dist/target/ (compiled output)
npm run buildcargo build --release
node app.jscargo run = build, then run the binary

Why? Rune draws 120 frames a second and does layout, text and springs on every one. That needs machine code, not an interpreter. You also want to hand someone a file that just runs.

How it works

cargo build downloads the source of every dependency (Rune, wgpu, winit, Taffy… several hundred crates), compiles each one, then compiles your code and links it all into one file. The first build is slow (1m 13s on our 6-core Mac). After that cargo reuses everything that didn't change, so a rebuild takes seconds.

There are two profiles:

  • debug (cargo build) → target/debug/. Fast to compile, slow to run, full of debug info. Ours measured 35 MB.
  • release (cargo build --release) → target/release/. Optimized: slower to compile, fast to run. Ours measured 24 MB.

Our Cargo.toml sets [profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2, so dependencies stay fast even in debug. Debug GPU code without it is painfully slow.

Where programs come from. Cargo finds programs by folder. Every file in src/bin/ becomes a binary named after the file (l1_switch.rs → target/release/l1_switch). Every file in examples/ becomes one you run with --example. src/lib.rs is a library the others import as rune_tutorial.

Key: the file in target/release/ is the program. It links only to frameworks that every Mac ships with. We checked with otool -L: AppKit, Metal, CoreText and others, all under /System/Library. So it runs on another Apple-silicon Mac with no Rust installed.

   …

    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 1m 13s
$ ls -lh target/release/l1_switch
-rwxr-xr-x  24M  target/release/l1_switch
$ file target/release/l1_switch
target/release/l1_switch: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64

Concept: state → view

Picture it first. A storyboard panel is drawn from the script, not from the previous panel. Change the script ("lights on") and the panel is redrawn to match.

What is it? State is Data, a plain struct with one bool. view is a Calculation: it borrows the state read-only (&State) and returns an El. It can't change anything, because Rust's borrow rules won't let it. on_press takes a closure that gets &mut State: that's the one Action.

Why? Because view is pure, Rune can call it as often as it likes, and you can call it in a test with no window (Lesson 5). Rust's types enforce the preference rule for you.

Three things on the switch you'll use in every lesson:

  • .key("knob"): a stable name. Rune matches old and new trees by key, so it knows this is the same knob that moved, not a new one.
  • .motion(motion::SNAPPY): changes in this subtree land on a 0.25 s spring. You change the number, and Rune animates it.
  • .role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on): what a screen reader announces ("Lights, switch, on"), through AccessKit. It's the same line of code, not a separate layer.

Why split it this way? knob_x is a Calculation pulled out of view. You can tell it's a calculation because it takes a bool, returns an f32 and touches nothing else. It's tiny, but it names the one number a spring animates, so Lesson 5's test can assert "lands 16 pt over" against knob_x(true) - knob_x(false).

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, motion, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, el, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Everything the app knows. Nothing else is stored anywhere.
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    on: bool,
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// Where the knob sits for a given switch position.
fn knob_x(on: bool) -> f32 {
    if on { 18.0 } else { 2.0 } // → points from the track's left edge
}

// The whole screen, described from the state. Rune calls this again after every change.
fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true); // → Theme (dark colours)
    let label = text(if s.on { "Lights on" } else { "Lights off" })
        .font(type_::TITLE)
        .color(t.text); // → El
    let knob = el().key("knob").size(18.0, 18.0).radius(9.0).fill(t.knob)
        .absolute(knob_x(s.on), 2.0); // → El
    let switch = el().key("switch")
        .role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on).focusable(true) // what a screen reader hears
        .size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
        .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
        .motion(motion::SNAPPY) // changes to this element and its children spring
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on) // the one Action: flip the bool
        .child(knob); // → El
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(16.0).fill(t.bg)
        .child(label)
        .child(switch) // → El (the root)
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("on", |s| s.on = true)], // named starting states for headless snaps
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 1 - Switch", (360.0, 220.0), State::default, view)
    });
}

Step 1.1 · Read and run (worked example)

No stub this time: you can't fill in the blanks of an app shape you've never seen. Read the code above top to bottom (imports → data → calculation → main), then build and run it with the commands in "Do it".

Step 1.2 · Work through it

  1. Change knob_x to return 14.0 for "on", then rebuild. Cargo recompiles only your crate, so the rebuild takes seconds, not a minute. Now the knob stops short.
  2. Swap motion::SNAPPY for rune::Spring::new(1.0, 0.5). A slow, bouncy knob shows that the spring is all there is to the animation.
  3. Run ./target/release/l1_switch --list-scenes. The scenes array in main is just named functions that set up the state.

Step 1.3 · Quiz yourself

  1. You email target/release/l1_switch to a friend with an Apple-silicon Mac and no Rust. Does it run? Would src/bin/l1_switch.rs run for them?
  2. You edit one string in l1_switch.rs. Why is the rebuild seconds when the first build was over a minute?
  3. Could view flip s.on itself? What stops you, the compiler or a convention?
  4. Delete .key("knob"). Predict whether the knob still slides, then try it.
✅ Solution (answers)
  1. Yes. It's a self-contained arm64 Mach-O that links only system frameworks. (macOS may warn that it's from an unidentified developer; Lesson 2 signs it.) The .rs file won't run: it's source code, and their machine has no compiler.
  2. Cargo caches each compiled crate under target/. Only rune-tutorial changed, so only it recompiles and re-links.
  3. The compiler. view receives &State, a shared borrow, and assigning through it is a compile error. Purity is enforced by the type system, not by discipline.
  4. Usually yes, here. With no key, Rune matches the knob by its position among its siblings, and here it's the only child. Keys matter when siblings reorder, which is Lesson 2.

Step 1.4 · Run it

cargo run --release --bin l1_switch

Expected output: a 360×220 dark window that says "Lights off", with a switch that flips and springs when you click it or press Space after Tab. If it fails: error: no bin target named means you're not in tutorial/. A compile error inside rune means your rev isn't 6231f17 (see the drift check).

✅ Lesson 1 complete. You've learned: what cargo builds and where, debug vs release, that a Rust binary stands alone, and the state → view → handler loop. Next: lay out a list, give rows identities, and turn the binary into a real Mac app.

Guided · Concepts: rows & columns, grow, keys, iterators, .app bundles

Layout, keys, and a real .app

A music queue whose rows slide to their new places, shipped as an app with a name in the menu bar.

Concept: flex layout

Picture it first. A magazine page is a grid of stacks: a column of articles, each a row of photo and text. When a headline gets longer, the layout reflows instead of you nudging every block.

What is it? row() lays its children out left to right and col() top to bottom. Underneath is Taffy, a real CSS flexbox engine, so .gap(), .padding(), .center_y() and .grow(1.0) mean what gap, padding, align-items: center and flex: 1 mean on the web. .absolute(x, y) takes a child out of the flow (Lesson 1's knob used it).

Why? Each queue row needs the title on the left and the length and button pinned right, whatever the title's length. Once the words column grows into the spare width, that happens for free.

Gotcha.grow() is flex: 1 1 0: an element is only as big as the free space its parent leaves. In a column with no fixed height there is none. The same rule bites on the web.

Concept: keys

Picture it first. Actors on a stage wear name tags. When the director reshuffles the line-up, everyone walks to their new mark. Without tags, the stage manager would just repaint whoever stands in spot 1 to look like the new spot-1 actor.

What is it? .key(..) is that name tag. Between two views Rune matches elements by key, so a keyed row that moves from 4th to 1st travels on its spring. Without keys it matches by position, and every row's text just swaps in place.

Teach by negative space: keying a row by its index (format!("row-{i}")) looks right and is wrong. After a reorder, "row-0" is a different track, so nothing travels. The key has to come from something about the item that doesn't change: track.id.

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, motion, radius, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Track {
    id: u32,
    title: &'static str,
    artist: &'static str,
    length: &'static str,
}

struct State {
    queue: Vec<Track>,
}

const TRACKS: [(&str, &str, &str); 5] = [
    ("Neon Rain", "Kiko Moss", "3:41"),
    ("Paper Planes", "The Lanterns", "2:58"),
    ("Slow Orbit", "Mira Vale", "4:12"),
    ("Glass Garden", "Odd Weather", "3:05"),
    ("Last Light", "Juno Park", "3:33"),
];

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        let queue = TRACKS.iter().zip(0..)
            .map(|(&(title, artist, length), id)| Track { id, title, artist, length })
            .collect(); // → Vec<Track>
        State { queue }
    }
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// CATEGORY: Calculation - a queue and an id in, a NEW queue out. No mutation.
fn play_next(queue: &[Track], id: u32) -> Vec<Track> { // in: &[Track], u32 → out: Vec<Track>
    // TODO(you) 1: put the track with `id` first and keep everyone else in their order.
    //   You can't mutate `queue` (it's borrowed, not owned). Which iterator adapters let you
    //   pick "the one" and "the rest" as two passes over the same slice, then join them?
    //   What does `Track` need to derive so you can turn `&Track` back into `Track`?
    let _ = (queue, id);
    todo!() // remove when implemented
}

// CATEGORY: Calculation - one track in, one row of elements out.
fn track_row(track: &Track, t: Theme) -> El { // in: &Track, Theme → out: El
    let id = track.id;
    // TODO(you) 2: title above artist. Which builder stacks children vertically? It must also
    //   take all the spare width so the length and button get pushed to the right edge -
    //   which flex property does that in CSS, and what is it called here?
    let words: El = todo!(); // remove when implemented
    let button = row().key("next").h(26.0).px(10.0).radius(13.0).center()
        .fill(t.control_off)
        .child(text("Play next").font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text))
        .on_press(move |s: &mut State| s.queue = play_next(&s.queue, id));
    row().h(52.0).px(14.0).gap(12.0).center_y().radius(radius::LG).fill(t.card)
        .child(words)
        .child(text(track.length).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .child(button)
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut list = col().gap(6.0);
    for track in &s.queue {
        // TODO(you) 3: give every row an identity that survives reordering. What is stable
        //   about a track that its position in the list is not? Try it with the row's index
        //   first, press "Play next", and watch what moves. Then fix it.
        list = list.child(track_row(track, t));
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().padding(20.0).pt(40.0).gap(14.0).fill(t.bg)
        .motion(motion::SMOOTH)
        .child(text("Up next").font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text))
        .child(list)
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::new("Exercise 2 - Up next", (420.0, 400.0), State::default, view));
}

Step 2.1 · Stub

The stub is on the right, and it's also examples/ex2_queue.rs. Pre-written: the data, the button and the page frame. Yours: play_next, the words column and the row key.

Step 2.2 · Work through it

TODO 1, play_next. Conceptual process: (1) it takes a borrowed slice, so you can't remove from it, which makes it a calculation by type; (2) "the picked one" then "the rest" is two filtered passes over the same slice; (3) chaining iterators joins them; (4) you're holding &Tracks and need Tracks, and the derive on the struct is the clue. Why this approach? A function that returns a new queue can be unit-tested with plain asserts, and the handler shrinks to one assignment.

TODO 2, the words column. Which builder stacks vertically, and which call makes it swallow the free width?

TODO 3, the key. Do the wrong version first (the index), run it, and watch the text swap without anything moving. Then key by id.

Step 2.3 · Quiz yourself

  1. Is play_next a Calculation or an Action? What in its signature tells you?
  2. The closure in on_press is move |s| …. What does it move in, and why can't it borrow track instead?
  3. Two tracks with the same id: what goes wrong on screen?
✅ Solution (consult after your attempt) 
// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, motion, radius, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Track {
    id: u32, // never changes, so it can name the row
    title: &'static str,
    artist: &'static str,
    length: &'static str,
}

struct State {
    queue: Vec<Track>,
}

const TRACKS: [(&str, &str, &str); 5] = [
    ("Neon Rain", "Kiko Moss", "3:41"),
    ("Paper Planes", "The Lanterns", "2:58"),
    ("Slow Orbit", "Mira Vale", "4:12"),
    ("Glass Garden", "Odd Weather", "3:05"),
    ("Last Light", "Juno Park", "3:33"),
];

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        let queue = TRACKS.iter().zip(0..)
            .map(|(&(title, artist, length), id)| Track { id, title, artist, length })
            .collect(); // → Vec<Track>
        State { queue }
    }
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// A new queue with track `id` at the front. Everything else keeps its order.
fn play_next(queue: &[Track], id: u32) -> Vec<Track> {
    let picked = queue.iter().filter(|t| t.id == id); // → the one track
    let rest = queue.iter().filter(|t| t.id != id); // → everyone else, in order
    picked.chain(rest).copied().collect() // → Vec<Track>
}

// One row: title and artist stacked on the left, length and a button on the right.
fn track_row(track: &Track, t: Theme) -> El {
    let id = track.id;
    let words = col().grow(1.0).gap(2.0) // grow: take the free width, push the rest right
        .child(text(track.title).font(type_::BODY).color(t.text))
        .child(text(track.artist).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary)); // → El
    let button = row().key("next").h(26.0).px(10.0).radius(13.0).center()
        .fill(t.control_off)
        .child(text("Play next").font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text))
        .on_press(move |s: &mut State| s.queue = play_next(&s.queue, id)); // the Action: replace the queue
    row().h(52.0).px(14.0).gap(12.0).center_y().radius(radius::LG).fill(t.card)
        .child(words)
        .child(text(track.length).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .child(button) // → El
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut list = col().gap(6.0); // → El
    for track in &s.queue {
        list = list.child(track_row(track, t).key(format!("track-{}", track.id))); // the identity
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().padding(20.0).pt(40.0).gap(14.0).fill(t.bg) // pt: clear the titlebar
        .motion(motion::SMOOTH)
        .child(text("Up next").font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text))
        .child(list) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::new("Lesson 2 - Up next", (420.0, 400.0), State::default, view));
}

Why this works: the view re-runs with the new order, and the keys let Rune see that the same five rows moved rather than five rows changing text.

Why split it this way?

  • play_next is a Calculation: a slice and an id in, a new Vec out, no I/O. It's extracted because it's the only real logic in the app, and it's now testable without Rune.
  • track_row is a Calculation too (it builds an El). It's extracted because view loops over it, and it keeps the loop to one line.
  • The handler is an Action, and it stays thin: one assignment. The decision lives in the calculation.

Quiz: (1) Calculation. It takes &[Track] and returns a value, with no &mut. (2) It moves the u32 id. The closure outlives this call to view, so it can't hold a borrow of data that only lives for one frame. (3) Two elements share a key, so Rune can't tell which is which, and the motion goes to the wrong row.

Concept: a .app is a folder

Picture it first. A film print in its can: the reel is the movie, and the label on the can tells the projectionist what it's called and how to run it. The binary is the reel, and the .app is the labelled can.

What is it? A macOS application bundle is a directory that ends in .app, which Finder shows as one icon. Inside, Contents/MacOS/ holds your executable and Contents/Info.plist (XML) gives its name, bundle id, and which file to run. codesign --sign - adds an ad-hoc signature. Apple Silicon refuses to run unsigned code, and "ad-hoc" means signed, but by nobody in particular.

Why? cargo run starts a bare binary: no app name in the menu bar, no Dock identity, and nothing to double-click. Rune's own README says the same, and it ships scripts/mac-app for the full version with icons, URL schemes and live relaunch. Ours is a deliberately small version: 20 lines you can read.

When NOT to extract: the script is one straight line of steps used for one job. It has no functions, no config file and no options beyond the two arguments, so splitting it would add names without removing any complexity. Reach for scripts/mac-app when you need an icon or signing with your developer ID.

$ cargo build --release --bin l2_queue
$ scripts/bundle-mac.sh l2_queue "Up Next"
built dist/Up Next.app
$ find "dist/Up Next.app" -type f
dist/Up Next.app/Contents/_CodeSignature/CodeResources
dist/Up Next.app/Contents/MacOS/l2_queue
dist/Up Next.app/Contents/Info.plist
$ codesign -v "dist/Up Next.app" && echo signed
signed
$ open "dist/Up Next.app"

Step 2.4 · Run it

cargo run --release --example ex2_queue
scripts/bundle-mac.sh l2_queue "Up Next" && open "dist/Up Next.app"

Expected output: your queue, where rows slide when you press "Play next". Then the bundle opens with "Up Next" in the menu bar. If it fails: a panic that names ex2_queue.rs points at the first unfinished todo!(). no target/release/l2_queue from the script means you skipped the build. macOS says the app "is damaged": the signing step failed, so check codesign -h.

✅ Lesson 2 complete. You've learned: flex rows and columns, why keys must come from identity rather than position, and what's inside a Mac app. Next: take control of the motion itself.

3

Guided · Concepts: springs, duration & bounce, enter/exit transitions

Springs and transitions

Three balls, three springs, one target, plus a word that knows how to arrive and how to leave.

Concept: springs, not timelines

Picture it first. A door closer. You don't program the door's path: you set how stiff the closer is, and wherever you let go of the door, it swings shut along a natural curve. Push it mid-swing and it changes direction smoothly, with no jump.

What is it? A spring is a physical model that moves a value toward a target. Spring::new(duration, bounce) describes it in designer units: about how long it takes to settle, and how much it overshoots (0 = none). Rune's tokens are named springs: SNAPPY (0.25 s, 0), PLAYFUL (0.25 s, 0.15), SMOOTH (0.32 s, 0).

Why? A CSS transition restarts from the current value with zero velocity, so a fast double-tap looks broken. A spring keeps its velocity when the target changes (retargeting), and that's what makes motion feel physical.

Concept: transitions

Picture it first. An actor's entrance and exit, rehearsed separately: walk in from stage left, exit through the trapdoor.

What is it? An element that appears or disappears between two views has presence. .transition(..) says how it enters and exits. Transition::offset(0, 10).combined(Transition::opacity()) rises and fades. Transition::asymmetric(enter, exit) uses different moves for each (Lesson 4). Exiting elements stay drawn until their exit finishes, so you just delete them from the state.

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, motion, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, Spring, Transition, col, el, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    right: bool, // which end of the track the balls are heading for
}

const TRACK_W: f32 = 300.0;
const BALL: f32 = 28.0;

// Name, spring. `Spring::new(duration in seconds, bounce from 0 to 1)`.
const LANES: [(&str, Spring); 3] = [
    ("SNAPPY", motion::SNAPPY),            // 0.25 s, no bounce
    ("PLAYFUL", motion::PLAYFUL),          // 0.25 s, a little bounce
    ("custom", Spring::new(0.8, 0.45)),    // slow and bouncy
];

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
fn ball_x(right: bool) -> f32 {
    if right { TRACK_W - BALL } else { 0.0 } // → points inside the track
}

fn lane(name: &str, spring: Spring, right: bool, t: Theme) -> El {
    let ball = el().key(format!("ball-{name}")).size(BALL, BALL).radius(BALL / 2.0)
        .fill(tok::accent(0, true))
        .absolute(ball_x(right), 0.0)
        .motion(spring); // this element's own spring → El
    col().gap(6.0)
        .child(text(name).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .child(el().w(TRACK_W).h(BALL).radius(BALL / 2.0).fill(t.control_off).child(ball)) // → El
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut lanes = col().gap(14.0);
    for (name, spring) in LANES {
        lanes = lanes.child(lane(name, spring, s.right, t));
    }
    let go = row().key("go").h(34.0).px(18.0).radius(17.0).center().fill(t.text)
        .press_scale(0.96)
        .child(text("Go").font(type_::BODY).color(t.bg))
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.right = !s.right); // → El
    let mut footer = row().h(34.0).gap(14.0).center_y().child(go);
    if s.right {
        // Mounted only while `right` is true: it enters and exits instead of popping.
        footer = footer.child(
            text("Wheee").key("wheee").font(type_::BODY).color(t.text)
                .transition(Transition::offset(0.0, 10.0).combined(Transition::opacity())),
        );
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(20.0).fill(t.bg)
        .child(lanes)
        .child(footer) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("right", |s| s.right = true)],
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 3 - Springs", (400.0, 300.0), State::default, view)
    });
}

Why split it this way? ball_x is a Calculation with a boundary worth naming (the far edge is TRACK_W - BALL). lane is a Calculation that builds one repeated piece. LANES is Data: making the springs a table, not three hand-written lanes, is the preference rule in action. Adding a lane is now a data edit, not a code edit.

Quiz: (1) Retargeting keeps the current position and velocity. (2) Every ball inherits the same spring, so all three move identically: inheritance goes down the tree, and the nearest .motion wins. (3) The element never leaves the tree, so it still takes layout space and screen-reader focus. Presence (mount and unmount) is what makes it truly gone.

Step 3.4 · Run it

cargo run --release --example ex3_springs

Expected output: three lanes, and Go sends the balls across on visibly different curves. If it fails: the balls jump, so the spring isn't attached to the ball (TODO 3). The ball pokes out of its track: ball_x forgot the ball's own width.

4

Guided · Concepts: on_drag, gesture phases, offset, thresholds

Drag

Swipe-to-archive notifications: they follow your finger exactly, and let go decides their fate.

Concept: a gesture has phases

Picture it first. A slingshot: grab, pull, release. What happens depends only on how far you pulled when you let go.

What is it? .on_drag(|s, d, tx| ..) runs once per phase of a pointer gesture: Phase::Down, then Move many times, then Up. d.dx/d.dy is how far the pointer has travelled since the press. Moves inside a drag land instantly, because the finger is the animation. The spring only takes over when you let go.

.offset(dx, 0) draws the card shifted without moving it in layout, so its neighbours hold still while you drag.

Why? Without phases you'd have to track "is the mouse down" yourself, which is state that goes stale the moment a release happens outside the window.

Teach by negative space: the tempting version puts if d.dx.abs() > 110.0 { remove } else { reset } straight in the Up arm. It works, and it hides your app's one real decision inside a closure that needs a live pointer to run. Pull it out into release(dx) -> Release, and the decision becomes a calculation you can test with one line (Lesson 5).

fn release(dx: f32) -> Release {
    if dx.abs() >= THRESHOLD { Release::Archive } else { Release::SnapBack } // → Release
}
.on_drag(move |s: &mut State, d: &mut Drag, _tx: &mut Tx| {
    let Some(i) = s.cards.iter().position(|c| c.id == id) else { return }; // → usize
    match d.phase {
        Phase::Down => {}
        Phase::Move => s.cards[i].dx = d.dx, // follows the hand, no spring
        Phase::Up => match release(d.dx) {
            Release::Archive => { s.cards.remove(i); } // exit transition flies it off
            Release::SnapBack => s.cards[i].dx = 0.0, // springs home
        },
    }
}) // → El

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, radius, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, Drag, El, Phase, Transition, Tx, col, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
struct Card {
    id: u32,
    title: &'static str,
    body: &'static str,
    dx: f32, // how far it's being dragged sideways, pt; 0 at rest
}

struct State {
    cards: Vec<Card>,
}

const THRESHOLD: f32 = 110.0; // let go past this and the card is archived

const NOTES: [(&str, &str); 4] = [
    ("Build finished", "main · 2m 14s · all checks passed"),
    ("New comment", "\"Ship it, the spring feels right\""),
    ("Calendar", "Design review in 15 minutes"),
    ("Battery low", "Plug in soon - 12% left"),
];

fn fresh_cards() -> Vec<Card> {
    NOTES.iter().zip(0..)
        .map(|(&(title, body), id)| Card { id, title, body, dx: 0.0 })
        .collect() // → Vec<Card>
}

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        State { cards: fresh_cards() }
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Release {
    Archive,
    SnapBack,
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// What a let-go means, from how far the card travelled. Either direction counts.
fn release(dx: f32) -> Release {
    if dx.abs() >= THRESHOLD { Release::Archive } else { Release::SnapBack } // → Release
}

// The card fades as it nears the threshold, so the hand can feel the commit point coming.
fn fade(dx: f32) -> f32 {
    1.0 - 0.6 * (dx.abs() / THRESHOLD).min(1.0) // → opacity 0.4..=1.0
}

fn card(c: &Card, t: Theme) -> El {
    let id = c.id;
    let away = if c.dx < 0.0 { -420.0 } else { 420.0 }; // leave the way it was thrown
    col().key(format!("card-{id}")).w_full().h(64.0).px(16.0).gap(4.0).justify_center()
        .radius(radius::LG).fill(t.card)
        .offset(c.dx, 0.0) // drawn shifted; layout (and its neighbours) stay put
        .opacity(fade(c.dx))
        .transition(Transition::asymmetric(Transition::opacity(), Transition::offset(away, 0.0)))
        .child(text(c.title).font(type_::BODY).color(t.text))
        .child(text(c.body).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .on_drag(move |s: &mut State, d: &mut Drag, _tx: &mut Tx| {
            let Some(i) = s.cards.iter().position(|c| c.id == id) else { return }; // → usize
            match d.phase {
                Phase::Down => {}
                Phase::Move => s.cards[i].dx = d.dx, // follows the hand, no spring
                Phase::Up => match release(d.dx) {
                    Release::Archive => { s.cards.remove(i); } // exit transition flies it off
                    Release::SnapBack => s.cards[i].dx = 0.0, // springs home
                },
            }
        }) // → El
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut list = col().w_full().gap(8.0);
    for c in &s.cards {
        list = list.child(card(c, t));
    }
    if s.cards.is_empty() {
        list = list.child(
            row().key("refill").h(36.0).px(14.0).radius(18.0).center().fill(t.control_off)
                .child(text("All clear. Bring them back").font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text))
                .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.cards = fresh_cards()),
        );
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().padding(20.0).pt(40.0).gap(14.0).fill(t.bg) // pt: clear the titlebar
        .child(text("Swipe to archive").font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text))
        .child(list) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::new("Lesson 4 - Swipe", (400.0, 380.0), State::default, view));
}

Why split it this way? release and fade are Calculations (numbers in, a value out). Release is Data: an enum names the two outcomes so a typo can't invent a third. The drag closure is the Action, and it never decides anything itself.

Quiz: (1) Presence: the removed element keeps drawing until its exit transition settles. (2) It's derived from data the view already has, so storing it would be a second copy that could disagree. (3) After an archive, indices shift, and a captured index would point at the next card.

Expected output: cards track your pointer 1:1, a short pull springs back, and a long one flies off and the rest close the gap. If it fails: the card lags behind the pointer, so you put a spring on the drag. Nothing archives on a left swipe: the sign.

5

Closer to solo · Concepts: Runtime, virtual clock, dependency injection, cargo test

Testing without a window

Drive Lesson 4 with a fake finger and a fake clock, and assert on both the state and the screen.

Concept: a headless runtime

Picture it first. A flight simulator: the real cockpit software, real instruments, but the "sky" is supplied by the test rig, one frame at a time.

What is it? rune::Runtime::new(state, view, size, env) runs your real view and Rune's real layout, springs and hit-testing, with no window and no GPU. You are the clock: rt.frame(1.0 / 60.0) advances it one frame. You are the finger: rt.pointer_down/move/up(x, y). You read the results with rt.state (the data), rt.find(key) (an element's centre) and rt.presented(key) (its drawn rect, mid-spring included).

Why? It's dependency injection. The app never reads the time or the mouse itself: Rune hands both in. So a test can hand in fake ones and get the same result every run, in milliseconds, on CI.

Test what a user would notice: "the card is gone" and "it's drawn back home", not "dx was set to 0". Then a refactor of the internals doesn't break the tests.

Tests sit in a #[cfg(test)] mod tests at the bottom of the same file. Only cargo test compiles them, so they never ship in the binary.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use rune::{Env, Runtime};

    // ── DATA ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    const SIZE: (f32, f32) = (400.0, 380.0);
    const DT: f64 = 1.0 / 60.0;

    // ── ACTIONS (on a fake window, not a real one) ──────────
    fn app() -> Runtime<State> {
        let env = Env { system_dark: true, scale: 2.0 };
        let mut rt = Runtime::new(State::default(), view, SIZE, env); // → Runtime<State>
        rt.frame(0.0); // build and lay out the first frame
        rt
    }

    // Press the element keyed `key`, move `dx` points over 10 frames, let go, let it settle.
    fn drag(rt: &mut Runtime<State>, key: &str, dx: f32) {
        let (x, y) = rt.find(key).expect("element on screen"); // → its centre, in points
        rt.pointer_down(x, y);
        for step in 1..=10 {
            rt.pointer_move(x + dx * step as f32 / 10.0, y);
            rt.frame(DT);
        }
        rt.pointer_up(x + dx, y);
        for _ in 0..60 {
            rt.frame(DT); // one second of springs
        }
    }

    // ── TESTS ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    #[test]
    fn release_archives_at_the_threshold_in_either_direction() {
        assert_eq!(release(THRESHOLD - 1.0), Release::SnapBack);
        assert_eq!(release(THRESHOLD), Release::Archive);
        assert_eq!(release(-THRESHOLD), Release::Archive);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_short_drag_springs_home() {
        let mut rt = app();
        let home = rt.presented("card-0").unwrap().0[0]; // → x of the drawn rect
        drag(&mut rt, "card-0", 60.0);
        assert_eq!(rt.state.cards.len(), 4, "nothing archived");
        let now = rt.presented("card-0").unwrap().0[0];
        assert!((now - home).abs() < 0.5, "back home: {home} → {now}");
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_long_drag_archives_the_card() {
        let mut rt = app();
        drag(&mut rt, "card-0", -180.0);
        let ids: Vec<u32> = rt.state.cards.iter().map(|c| c.id).collect(); // → [1, 2, 3]
        assert_eq!(ids, [1, 2, 3]);
        assert!(rt.find("card-0").is_none(), "gone from the screen too");
    }
}

Quiz: (1) Each frame delivers one Move phase. One jump is one move, and the press-to-drag threshold and the follow behaviour are never exercised. (2) Pulling release out as a calculation in Lesson 4. (3) Only rt.frame(dt), which is fixed, so it's not time. Look for something nondeterministic you introduced, like a HashMap iteration order.

6

Closer to solo · Concepts: effect slots, compositor, effect_data, bleed

GPU effects: fire

The view marks a box. A compositor paints fire into it on the GPU, and you steer it with four numbers.

Concept: effect slots

Picture it first. A green screen on set. The actors (your UI) are filmed around a green rectangle, and in post the VFX house fills it with fire. The rectangle is cheap, and the fire is someone else's pipeline.

What is it? rune::effect(MARK) is an element that draws nothing. It just reserves a box in the paint order. A compositor (src/gfx.rs, adapted from Rune's showreel) runs every frame, finds each slot, reads its mark (which effect) and its .effect_data([f32; 4]) (four numbers), and asks rune-fx to paint that effect there with wgpu. .effect_bleed(pt) lets the effect draw outside the box. Flames rise far above a 24-pt slot. rune::run_with(spec, Gfx::default()) attaches the compositor.

Why? UI elements are rectangles, text and gradients. Fire is a fluid simulation. The slot lets the declarative view say where and how much, and leaves the how to a shader.

Paint order is z-order: later children draw on top. Put the log after the fire and it sits in front of the flames.

Read: the projector (src/gfx.rs)

You don't write this file. Read just two parts. The marks are Data, the contract between your view and the compositor. layer is a Calculation that turns one slot's mark and numbers into one rune-fx layer. The rest is the Action that talks to the GPU.

Two bugs we already hitA slot smaller than 1 pt sends NaNs into the shaders, so gfx.rs skips it. And software GPUs (a Linux VM's lavapipe) render these effects differently from Metal, so judge effects on real hardware.
/// Fire rising off the slot's top edge. data: [flame height pt, intensity, 0, 0]
pub const FIRE: u32 = 1;
/// Liquid glass, gooey-unioned with an optional circle. data: [circle x, y, r (0 = none), frost]
pub const LENS: u32 = 2;
/// A ring of distortion through everything drawn before it. data: [x, y, start time s, amount]
pub const SHOCK: u32 = 3;
fn layer(mark: u32, d: [f32; 4], shape: Shape, t: f32) -> Option<FxLayer> {
    let fx = match mark {
        FIRE => Fx::fire(FireParams {
            height: d[0],
            intensity: d[1],
            embers: 24,
            scale: 24.0,
            ..FireParams::default()
        }),
        LENS => Fx::lens(LensParams {
            second: (d[2] > 0.0).then(|| Shape::circle(d[0], d[1], d[2])), // → Option<Shape>
            frost: d[3],
            bevel: 12.0,
            depth: 18.0,
            dispersion: 0.22,
            magnification: 1.08,
            union_k: 24.0,
            shadow: 0.0, // the shadow follows the goo and drags a dark box behind it
            ..Default::default()
        }),
        SHOCK => Fx::distort(DistortParams::Shockwave {
            at: [d[0], d[1]],
            reach: 700.0,
            width: 70.0,
            amount: d[3],
            chroma: 0.6,
            t0: d[2],
            duration: 1.0,
        }),
        _ => return None,
    };
    Some(fx.on(shape).at(t)) // → FxLayer
}

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, el, row, text};
use rune_tutorial::gfx::{FIRE, Gfx};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    heat: u32, // 0 = embers, 3 = roaring
}

const W: f32 = 420.0;
const H: f32 = 320.0;
const LOG_Y: f32 = 230.0;

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// The numbers the fire shader reads, from how hot the fire is.
fn flames(heat: u32) -> [f32; 4] {
    let k = heat as f32 / 3.0; // → 0.0..=1.0
    [24.0 + 110.0 * k, 0.5 + 0.8 * k, 0.0, 0.0] // → [height pt, intensity, unused, unused]
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let fire = rune::effect(FIRE) // a box that draws nothing; the compositor paints here
        .effect_data(flames(s.heat)) // four numbers for the shader
        .effect_bleed(200.0) // flames rise past the slot's top edge
        .absolute(110.0, LOG_Y)
        .size(200.0, 24.0); // → El
    let log = el().absolute(120.0, LOG_Y + 6.0).size(180.0, 20.0).radius(10.0)
        .fill(rune::color::hex("#3b2416").unwrap()); // → El
    let stoke = row().key("stoke").h(32.0).px(16.0).radius(16.0).center().fill(t.control_off)
        .child(text(if s.heat < 3 { "Stoke the fire" } else { "Let it settle" }).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text))
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.heat = (s.heat + 1) % 4); // → El
    el().w(W).h(H).fill(rune::color::hex("#0c0b0d").unwrap())
        .child(fire)
        .child(log) // drawn after the fire, so the log sits in front of the flames
        .child(col().absolute(0.0, 40.0).w(W).center().gap(10.0)
            .child(text(format!("Heat {} of 3", s.heat)).font(type_::BODY).color(t.text))
            .child(stoke)) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    let spec = AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("roaring", |s| s.heat = 3)],
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 6 - Campfire", (W, H), State::default, view)
    };
    rune::run_with(spec, Gfx::default()); // run, plus a compositor for the effect slots
}

When NOT to extract: log stays an inline let, not a fn log(). It's used once, takes no input and has no logic, so a function would add a name and remove nothing. flames earns its function: it holds the one mapping you'll want to tune and test.

Quiz: (1) flames, yes. Drawing is an Action owned by the compositor, outside your app code. (2) The slot's payload travels with Rune's per-instance GPU data, which is a fixed four floats. The marks table documents what each one means. (3) The flames are cut off at the slot's top edge.

7

Closer to solo · Concepts: backdrop effects, gooey union, Tx::instant

Liquid glass

A glass pill that bends the stripes behind it, and a drop you can pull out that clings like water.

Concept: effects that read the backdrop

Picture it first. A magnifying glass on a newspaper. The glass has no picture of its own: it bends the print beneath it. Move the paper, and the glass shows the new print.

What is it? .effect_backdrop(true) marks a slot that needs to read everything drawn before it. Rune pauses the frame there, copies what's been drawn so far, hands the copy to the compositor, then carries on. The LENS effect refracts that copy through a bevelled shape. Give it a second circle and the two shapes merge with a smooth union, the gooey bridge you see when the drop is close. It's the same math that makes metaballs.

Why? A backdrop read costs a pause and a copy, so it's opt-in per slot. Ordinary slots never pay for it.

tx.instant() inside the Move arm lands the drag change without a spring. This handler moves the effect's data, not an element with drag-follow built in, so you say it yourself.

Gotcha we hitrune-fx's lens draws a drop shadow by default, and the shadow follows the goo: a dark rectangle trails the drop. gfx.rs sets shadow: 0.0. It only showed in a live window, not in still snaps.

const DROP_R: f32 = 18.0;

    // TODO(you) 1: at rest the drop hangs just under the pill's right end, half inside it.
    //   Start from PILL's x, y, w, h. Then add the pull.
    let _ = pull;
    todo!() // remove when implemented
}

fn stripes() -> El {
    let mut r = row().absolute(0.0, 0.0).size(W, H).gap(12.0).justify_center();
    for i in 0..22 {
        let hex = ["#ff5ca8", "#7c5cff", "#22d3ee", "#ffb547"][i % 4];
        r = r.child(el().w(8.0).h_full().fill(rune::color::hex(hex).unwrap()));
    }

}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let (x, y, w, h) = PILL;

        .effect_data([cx, cy, DROP_R, 0.1])

        .radius(DROP_R)

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, Drag, El, Phase, Tx, el, row, text};
use rune_tutorial::gfx::{Gfx, LENS};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    pull: (f32, f32), // how far the drop is dragged from home, pt
}

const W: f32 = 420.0;
const H: f32 = 320.0;
const PILL: (f32, f32, f32, f32) = (110.0, 130.0, 200.0, 56.0); // x, y, w, h
const DROP_R: f32 = 18.0;

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// Where the drop's centre is: just under the pill's right end, plus the pull.
fn drop_centre(pull: (f32, f32)) -> (f32, f32) {
    let (x, y, w, h) = PILL;
    (x + w - 40.0 + pull.0, y + h - 6.0 + pull.1) // → window points
}

fn stripes() -> El {
    let mut r = row().absolute(0.0, 0.0).size(W, H).gap(12.0).justify_center();
    for i in 0..22 {
        let hex = ["#ff5ca8", "#7c5cff", "#22d3ee", "#ffb547"][i % 4];
        r = r.child(el().w(8.0).h_full().fill(rune::color::hex(hex).unwrap()));
    }
    r // → El: something for the glass to bend
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let (x, y, w, h) = PILL;
    let (cx, cy) = drop_centre(s.pull);
    let glass = rune::effect(LENS)
        .effect_data([cx, cy, DROP_R, 0.1]) // the drop: a circle gooey-unioned to the pill
        .effect_backdrop(true) // this slot reads what was drawn before it
        .absolute(x, y).size(w, h).radius(h / 2.0); // → El
    // An invisible handle over the drop, to grab it with.
    let handle = el().key("drop").absolute(cx - DROP_R, cy - DROP_R).size(2.0 * DROP_R, 2.0 * DROP_R)
        .radius(DROP_R)
        .on_drag(|s: &mut State, d: &mut Drag, tx: &mut Tx| match d.phase {
            Phase::Down => {}
            Phase::Move => {
                s.pull = (d.dx, d.dy);
                tx.instant();
            }
            Phase::Up => s.pull = (0.0, 0.0),
        }); // → El
    el().w(W).h(H).fill(rune::color::hex("#0d0a14").unwrap())
        .child(stripes())
        .child(glass)
        .child(handle)
        .child(row().absolute(0.0, 40.0).w(W).center()
            .child(row().h(30.0).px(14.0).radius(15.0).center().fill(t.bg)
                .child(text("Pull the drop out of the glass").font(type_::BODY).color(t.text)))) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    let spec = AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("pulled", |s| s.pull = (40.0, 70.0))],
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 7 - Liquid glass", (W, H), State::default, view)
    };
    rune::run_with(spec, Gfx::default());
}

Quiz: (1) Just the plain background. The backdrop is only what was drawn before the slot. (2) The Up commit isn't instant, so the handle element springs on its default motion, and the slot's data follows the view, which the runtime re-runs while the spring is in flight.

Step 7.4 · Run it

cargo run --release --example ex7_glass

Expected output: bent stripes inside the pill, and a drop that stretches out with a neck, snaps free, and springs home. If it fails: a flat dark pill means no backdrop flag. A drop that lags your pointer: no instant.

✅ Lesson 7 complete. You've learned: backdrop reads, smooth unions, and choosing instant vs sprung per commit. Next: effects driven by time.

8

Solo · Concepts: poll, the clock as data, start times over timers

Shockwave and the clock

Press a button and a ring of distortion ripples through every tile on screen.

Concept: store when, not how far along

Picture it first. A stopwatch photo. You don't keep updating a note that says "the race is 3.2 s old": you write down when the gun went off, and anyone with a clock can work out the rest.

What is it? AppSpec::poll is a function Rune calls every frame with the current time. It's an Action (it depends on when it runs), and it's the only place your app touches the clock. Copy now into the state there. The handler records fired_at = s.now, and the shader gets fired_at and computes the ring's radius itself from the compositor's own time.

Teach by negative space: the tempting design is a progress: f32 that poll nudges up every frame. It drifts if a frame is skipped, it needs a "done" flag, and it forces the view to rebuild 60 times a second. A start time is one number, written once. Rune only runs frames, and so poll, while something asks for them, so poll calls tx.wake_after(Duration::ZERO) to ask for the next one. Without it a press can stamp a stale now. poll returns false because nothing the view draws changed: the GPU animates on its own, since the compositor reports animating() = true.

DI again: because poll receives now instead of reading the system clock, a headless run (and a test) controls time completely. That's why the recording on the right is identical every time we render it.

// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, Tx, el, row, text};
use rune_tutorial::gfx::{Gfx, SHOCK};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
struct State {
    now: f64,
    fired_at: f64,
}

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        // TODO(you) 1: what should `fired_at` start as so that NO wave plays at launch?
        //   (The shader plays a wave for about a second after `fired_at`.)
        State { now: 0.0, fired_at: 0.0 }
    }
}

const W: f32 = 420.0;
const H: f32 = 320.0;
const BUTTON: (f32, f32, f32, f32) = (150.0, 140.0, 120.0, 40.0);

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
fn tiles() -> El {
    let mut root = el().absolute(0.0, 0.0).size(W, H);
    for i in 0..30 {
        let (x, y) = ((i % 6) as f32 * 70.0 + 6.0, (i / 6) as f32 * 64.0 + 6.0);
        root = root.child(el().absolute(x, y).size(58.0, 52.0).radius(8.0)
            .fill(rune::color::hex("#1d1a24").unwrap()));
    }
    root
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let (x, y, w, h) = BUTTON;
    // TODO(you) 2: on press, remember WHEN. Handlers get `&mut State` only - no clock.
    //   Where does the current time come from, then?
    let button = row().key("boom").absolute(x, y).size(w, h).radius(h / 2.0).center()
        .fill(tok::accent(0, true)).press_scale(0.94)
        .child(text("Boom").font(type_::BODY).color(t.bg));
    // TODO(you) 3: a SHOCK slot over the whole window, centred on the button, reading the
    //   backdrop. Data is [x, y, start time, strength]. Must it be the first child or the last?
    let wave: El = el();
    let _ = (SHOCK, s.fired_at, s.now);
    el().w(W).h(H).fill(rune::color::hex("#0b0b0d").unwrap())
        .child(tiles())
        .child(button)
        .child(wave)
}

// ── 4. ACTIONS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
// CATEGORY: Action - depends on WHEN it runs (it reads the clock).
fn poll(s: &mut State, now: f64, _: &mut Tx) -> bool { // in: &mut State, f64 → out: bool
    // TODO(you) 4: keep the state's clock current. Rune only draws (and polls) while something
    //   asks for frames - which `Tx` call asks for the next one? Then the return value: the
    //   view only needs rebuilding when something it draws changed. Did it?
    let _ = (s, now);
    todo!() // remove when implemented
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    let spec = AppSpec::<State> {
        poll: Some(poll),
        ..AppSpec::new("Exercise 8 - Shockwave", (W, H), State::default, view)
    };
    rune::run_with(spec, Gfx::default());
}

Step 8.3 · Quiz yourself

  1. Why must the SHOCK slot be the last child?
  2. What happens if fired_at starts at 0.0?
  3. poll returns true forever. What does it cost, and who notices?
✅ Solution (consult after your attempt) 
// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, type_};
use std::time::Duration;
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, Tx, col, el, row, text};
use rune_tutorial::gfx::{Gfx, SHOCK};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
struct State {
    now: f64,      // seconds on Rune's clock, copied in by `poll`
    fired_at: f64, // when the last wave started; far in the past = no wave
}

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        State { now: 0.0, fired_at: -10.0 }
    }
}

const W: f32 = 420.0;
const H: f32 = 320.0;
const BUTTON: (f32, f32, f32, f32) = (150.0, 140.0, 120.0, 40.0);

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
fn button_centre() -> (f32, f32) {
    let (x, y, w, h) = BUTTON;
    (x + w / 2.0, y + h / 2.0) // → window points
}

fn tiles() -> El {
    let mut root = el().absolute(0.0, 0.0).size(W, H);
    for i in 0..30 {
        let (x, y) = ((i % 6) as f32 * 70.0 + 6.0, (i / 6) as f32 * 64.0 + 6.0);
        root = root.child(el().absolute(x, y).size(58.0, 52.0).radius(8.0)
            .fill(rune::color::hex("#1d1a24").unwrap()));
    }
    root // → El: a grid for the wave to bend
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let (x, y, w, h) = BUTTON;
    let (cx, cy) = button_centre();
    let button = row().key("boom").absolute(x, y).size(w, h).radius(h / 2.0).center()
        .fill(tok::accent(0, true)).press_scale(0.94)
        .child(text("Boom").font(type_::BODY).color(t.bg))
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.fired_at = s.now); // the Action: remember when
    let wave = rune::effect(SHOCK)
        .effect_data([cx, cy, s.fired_at as f32, 14.0]) // [x, y, start time, strength]
        .effect_backdrop(true)
        .absolute(0.0, 0.0).size(W, H); // → El, last so it bends everything above
    el().w(W).h(H).fill(rune::color::hex("#0b0b0d").unwrap())
        .child(tiles())
        .child(col().absolute(0.0, 240.0).w(W).center()
            .child(text("Every tile under the ring bends").font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary)))
        .child(button)
        .child(wave) // → El
}

// ── 4. ACTIONS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
// Called every frame with Rune's clock. Returns whether anything visible changed.
fn poll(s: &mut State, now: f64, tx: &mut Tx) -> bool {
    s.now = now;
    tx.wake_after(Duration::ZERO); // ask for the next frame, so `now` never goes stale
    false // nothing the view draws changed; the GPU animates the wave on its own
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    let spec = AppSpec::<State> {
        poll: Some(poll),
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 8 - Shockwave", (W, H), State::default, view)
    };
    rune::run_with(spec, Gfx::default());
}

Quiz: (1) It distorts what was drawn before it, so anything after it is untouched. (2) A wave plays at launch, because time 0 is "just now". (3) The view rebuilds every frame for nothing: wasted CPU, and on a laptop, battery. Rune's own guidance is that poll returns true only when visible state changed.

Step 8.4 · Run it

cargo run --release --example ex8_shock

Expected output: a calm grid, and each Boom sends one ring out across the window. If it fails: a wave at launch means the fired_at default. A wave that starts late, or not at all, means poll isn't asking for frames, so now is stale when you press.

✅ Lesson 8 complete. You've learned: poll as the one clock Action, start times over counters, and backdrop distortion. Next: the closing checks.

Test plan

  1. Setup: cd tutorial && cargo --version → 1.99.1.
  2. cargo build --release --bins → Finished, exit 0.
  3. cargo build --examples → Finished, exit 0. Your exercises compile.
  4. cargo test --release --bin l4_swipe and cargo test --example ex5_tests → 3 passed each.
  5. Open each of your exercises with cargo run --release --example exN_…, and compare it to its recording on this page.
  6. scripts/bundle-mac.sh l2_queue "Up Next" && open "dist/Up Next.app" → the menu bar says "Up Next".
  7. Teardown: rm -rf dist (and cargo clean if you need the disk back: target/ runs to gigabytes).

A unit test for every view would be disproportionate. Lesson 5's three tests cover the one decision with a boundary. Verify the visual lessons by running them next to the recordings.

Done criteria

Per step

  • L1: file target/release/l1_switch prints Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
  • L2: codesign -v "dist/Up Next.app" exits 0
  • L3: cargo run --release --example ex3_springs shows three lanes moving on different curves
  • L4: grep -c todo! examples/ex4_swipe.rs prints 0 and the cards swipe
  • L5: cargo test --example ex5_tests → 3 passed
  • L6: grep -c todo! examples/ex6_fire.rs → 0, and flames grow on stoke
  • L7: grep -c effect_backdrop examples/ex7_glass.rs → 1, and the stripes bend
  • L8: grep -c todo! examples/ex8_shock.rs → 0, and no wave at launch

Final gates

  • cargo build --release --bins --examples exits 0
  • cargo clippy --release --examples shows no errors
  • cargo test --release → every suite passes
  • git status --short lists only files under tutorial/examples/ (or your new src/bin/ files)
  • git status --short --ignored | grep -E 'target|dist' shows them as ignored (!!), never staged

STOP conditions

Stop and ask instead of improvising when
  • Drift: the rev in Cargo.toml isn't 6231f17…, or a method name on this page doesn't exist (no method named … found for struct El).
  • Symptom unchanged after the fix: you changed the code and the window looks the same, which usually means you're running a different binary (--bin vs --example) than the one you edited.
  • You find yourself editing src/gfx.rs or anything in Rune to make an exercise work.
  • An effect looks wrong only on a VM or Linux software GPU: that's a known rendering difference, not your bug.
  • macOS blocks the .app, and the fix seems to involve disabling Gatekeeper or System Integrity Protection. Don't.

Maintenance notes

  • Rune is pre-release, and its dev branch moves daily. Bumping the rev is a deliberate act: change both lines, run the Test plan, and rebuild this page (python3 build.py). Snippets are cut from the compiled files, so a renamed API fails the build, not the reader.
  • The recordings are made on a Mac (Metal) with each lesson's --script scripts/lN.json --video media/lN.mp4 --scale 2. Re-record after a rev bump, because effects can change between revs.
  • Deferred: Windows/Linux bundling, app icons and Developer ID signing (see Stretch Goals), and the web target.
  • Reviewer: check that every // @snip has a matching // @end (build.py asserts it), and that examples/ex5_tests.rs was regenerated.

What you should know now

You can now do, unaided

  • Turn a folder of Rust source into a standalone executable, say where cargo put it, and explain why it runs on a machine without Rust.
  • Wrap that executable into a signed .app by hand, and read any .app's Info.plist to see what it runs.
  • Build a screen from state with rows, columns and keys, and predict which elements will travel and which will swap in place.
  • Choose a spring or a transition by feel, and explain why a spring survives a double tap.
  • Write a headless test that drags an element and asserts on both state and pixels.
  • Add a GPU effect to a view by reserving a slot and feeding it four numbers.

Now true about this codebase

  • Every file in tutorial/src/bin/ is its own program, and rune_tutorial::gfx is the only shared code.
  • The compositor's marks table (FIRE = 1, LENS = 2, SHOCK = 3) is the contract between views and effects. Adding an effect means a new mark and a new layer arm, and nothing in the views.
  • Every snippet on this page is extracted from code that compiles. Edit the .rs, not the HTML.

Check yourself

  1. A friend's copy of your .app opens, but on their Intel Mac it says "bad CPU type". What did you build for, and what would you change?
  2. A list reorder looks like the text "flickers" instead of rows moving. What's your first grep?
  3. A progress ring you added makes the laptop fan spin even when idle. Which function do you open first?

Advanced techniques & alternate solutions

Bundling: cargo-bundle or Rune's scripts/mac-app

cargo install cargo-bundle     # reads [package.metadata.bundle] from Cargo.toml
cargo bundle --release --bin l2_queue

It wins when you ship to several platforms (it also makes .deb and .msi) and want the metadata in Cargo.toml. Rune's scripts/mac-app wins on a Mac you're iterating on: it relaunches without the window blinking and keeps permissions. Our 20-line script is worse for shipping but better for learning, because there's nothing in it you can't read. The crossover is the first time you need an icon.

Animating by hand from poll

fn poll(s: &mut State, now: f64, _: &mut Tx) -> bool {
    s.x += (target(s) - s.x) * 0.2;   // a hand-rolled ease, every frame
    true
}

Worse here: it ties motion to frame rate, loses velocity on retarget, and rebuilds the view every frame. It wins when the motion is the content, like a physics toy or a game loop, where you need full control of every step. The falling todo in the repo's own "floor is lava" experiment does exactly this. It also has to call tx.instant() in poll, because Rune would otherwise spring-smooth every keyed position it sets by hand.

Keeping decisions in handlers

For a two-line app with no tests, an inline if in the handler is fine, and extracting release would be ceremony. The crossover is the first time you want to test the rule, or a second gesture (a keyboard shortcut, say) needs the same decision.

Considered and rejected for this page: the web build

Rune can target one WebGPU canvas, which would make these examples interactive in the page. When we tried it, Chrome and Helium clipped the canvas and dropped the effects. Recordings of the real native build were the approach we could verify end to end.

Reference

Common patterns

  • Calculation returns new data → handler assigns it (s.queue = play_next(&s.queue, id)).
  • Key by identity: .key(format!("track-{}", track.id)).
  • Drag: Move sets an offset, and Up asks a calculation and applies its answer.
  • Time: poll copies now, and handlers store start times.
  • Effect: rune::effect(MARK).effect_data([..]).absolute(..).size(..), plus run_with.

Key takeaways

  • target/release/<name> is the program, and a .app is a folder around it.
  • The view is a calculation by type, and the compiler keeps it pure.
  • Motion is a property (a spring), never a script.
  • Inject the clock and the pointer, and everything becomes testable.

Troubleshooting

Problem: error[E0599]: no method named … for struct El.
Solution: rev drift, or a typo. Check the drift check, then the method list in Rune's crates/rune/README.md at the pinned rev.

Problem: the first build fails while compiling objc2 or metal.
Solution: run xcode-select --install (Command Line Tools).

Problem: --video fails at once.
Solution: ffmpeg isn't on PATH (brew install ffmpeg).

Problem: text sits under the traffic lights.
Solution: windows draw under the titlebar, so add .pt(40.0) to your root column.

Problem: springs snap instantly in a window but glide in headless recordings.
Solution: macOS Reduce Motion is on (System Settings → Accessibility → Display). Rune honours it by snapping travel to a short fade. Headless runs don't read it.

Problem: a dark box trails a glass shape.
Solution: the lens shadow, so set shadow: 0.0 in its LensParams.

Full reference implementation

Lesson 1 · src/bin/l1_switch.rs
// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, motion, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, el, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Everything the app knows. Nothing else is stored anywhere.
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    on: bool,
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// Where the knob sits for a given switch position.
fn knob_x(on: bool) -> f32 {
    if on { 18.0 } else { 2.0 } // → points from the track's left edge
}

// The whole screen, described from the state. Rune calls this again after every change.
fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true); // → Theme (dark colours)
    let label = text(if s.on { "Lights on" } else { "Lights off" })
        .font(type_::TITLE)
        .color(t.text); // → El
    let knob = el().key("knob").size(18.0, 18.0).radius(9.0).fill(t.knob)
        .absolute(knob_x(s.on), 2.0); // → El
    let switch = el().key("switch")
        .role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on).focusable(true) // what a screen reader hears
        .size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
        .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
        .motion(motion::SNAPPY) // changes to this element and its children spring
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on) // the one Action: flip the bool
        .child(knob); // → El
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(16.0).fill(t.bg)
        .child(label)
        .child(switch) // → El (the root)
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("on", |s| s.on = true)], // named starting states for headless snaps
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 1 - Switch", (360.0, 220.0), State::default, view)
    });
}
Lesson 2 · src/bin/l2_queue.rs
// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, motion, radius, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, col, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Track {
    id: u32, // never changes, so it can name the row
    title: &'static str,
    artist: &'static str,
    length: &'static str,
}

struct State {
    queue: Vec<Track>,
}

const TRACKS: [(&str, &str, &str); 5] = [
    ("Neon Rain", "Kiko Moss", "3:41"),
    ("Paper Planes", "The Lanterns", "2:58"),
    ("Slow Orbit", "Mira Vale", "4:12"),
    ("Glass Garden", "Odd Weather", "3:05"),
    ("Last Light", "Juno Park", "3:33"),
];

impl Default for State {
    fn default() -> Self {
        let queue = TRACKS.iter().zip(0..)
            .map(|(&(title, artist, length), id)| Track { id, title, artist, length })
            .collect(); // → Vec<Track>
        State { queue }
    }
}

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
// A new queue with track `id` at the front. Everything else keeps its order.
fn play_next(queue: &[Track], id: u32) -> Vec<Track> {
    let picked = queue.iter().filter(|t| t.id == id); // → the one track
    let rest = queue.iter().filter(|t| t.id != id); // → everyone else, in order
    picked.chain(rest).copied().collect() // → Vec<Track>
}

// One row: title and artist stacked on the left, length and a button on the right.
fn track_row(track: &Track, t: Theme) -> El {
    let id = track.id;
    let words = col().grow(1.0).gap(2.0) // grow: take the free width, push the rest right
        .child(text(track.title).font(type_::BODY).color(t.text))
        .child(text(track.artist).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary)); // → El
    let button = row().key("next").h(26.0).px(10.0).radius(13.0).center()
        .fill(t.control_off)
        .child(text("Play next").font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text))
        .on_press(move |s: &mut State| s.queue = play_next(&s.queue, id)); // the Action: replace the queue
    row().h(52.0).px(14.0).gap(12.0).center_y().radius(radius::LG).fill(t.card)
        .child(words)
        .child(text(track.length).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .child(button) // → El
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut list = col().gap(6.0); // → El
    for track in &s.queue {
        list = list.child(track_row(track, t).key(format!("track-{}", track.id))); // the identity
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().padding(20.0).pt(40.0).gap(14.0).fill(t.bg) // pt: clear the titlebar
        .motion(motion::SMOOTH)
        .child(text("Up next").font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text))
        .child(list) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::new("Lesson 2 - Up next", (420.0, 400.0), State::default, view));
}
Lesson 3 · src/bin/l3_springs.rs
// ── 1. IMPORTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────
use rune::tok::{self, Theme, motion, type_};
use rune::{AppSpec, Cx, El, Spring, Transition, col, el, row, text};

// ── 2. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#[derive(Default)]
struct State {
    right: bool, // which end of the track the balls are heading for
}

const TRACK_W: f32 = 300.0;
const BALL: f32 = 28.0;

// Name, spring. `Spring::new(duration in seconds, bounce from 0 to 1)`.
const LANES: [(&str, Spring); 3] = [
    ("SNAPPY", motion::SNAPPY),            // 0.25 s, no bounce
    ("PLAYFUL", motion::PLAYFUL),          // 0.25 s, a little bounce
    ("custom", Spring::new(0.8, 0.45)),    // slow and bouncy
];

// ── 3. CALCULATION ──────────────────────────────────────────
fn ball_x(right: bool) -> f32 {
    if right { TRACK_W - BALL } else { 0.0 } // → points inside the track
}

fn lane(name: &str, spring: Spring, right: bool, t: Theme) -> El {
    let ball = el().key(format!("ball-{name}")).size(BALL, BALL).radius(BALL / 2.0)
        .fill(tok::accent(0, true))
        .absolute(ball_x(right), 0.0)
        .motion(spring); // this element's own spring → El
    col().gap(6.0)
        .child(text(name).font(type_::LABEL).color(t.text_secondary))
        .child(el().w(TRACK_W).h(BALL).radius(BALL / 2.0).fill(t.control_off).child(ball)) // → El
}

fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let mut lanes = col().gap(14.0);
    for (name, spring) in LANES {
        lanes = lanes.child(lane(name, spring, s.right, t));
    }
    let go = row().key("go").h(34.0).px(18.0).radius(17.0).center().fill(t.text)
        .press_scale(0.96)
        .child(text("Go").font(type_::BODY).color(t.bg))
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.right = !s.right); // → El
    let mut footer = row().h(34.0).gap(14.0).center_y().child(go);
    if s.right {
        // Mounted only while `right` is true: it enters and exits instead of popping.
        footer = footer.child(
            text("Wheee").key("wheee").font(type_::BODY).color(t.text)
                .transition(Transition::offset(0.0, 10.0).combined(Transition::opacity())),
        );
    }
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(20.0).fill(t.bg)
        .child(lanes)
        .child(footer) // → El
}

// ── 5. MAIN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fn main() {
    rune::run(AppSpec::<State> {
        scenes: &[("right", |s| s.right = true)],
        ..AppSpec::new("Lesson 3 - Springs", (400.0, 300.0), State::default, view)
    });
}
